reading.rtitle: The Session You Would Book If Nobody Was Watching
paras: There is a question worth asking anybody who has done a job for more than five years, and it sounds like small talk until you hear the answer. If you had a clean slate, and the same budget, what would you do differently? Almost everybody says the same thing first: I would start from scratch. And almost everybody is wrong, because what they actually describe next is never the whole system. It is two or three specific decisions that were made badly in the first month and that everything since has been built on top of.

The second thing people say is more interesting, because it is where the constraints show up. If I had more time, I would rehearse for two days instead of one. If the budget were bigger, I would hire a second engineer. These sound like complaints, and they are not: they are a map of exactly where the work is being damaged, drawn by the only person who can see it. A producer who says she would swap one piece of equipment is telling you something very small. A producer who says she would swap the order of the whole week is telling you that the process itself is upside down.

The third answer is the one that costs something to say out loud. In hindsight, I would not have argued about it. In hindsight, I would have said no in March. People are far more honest about their own mistakes when the sentence is hypothetical, which is why the question works. If somebody asks what you did wrong, you defend yourself. If somebody asks what you would do differently, you tell the truth, and the two questions are almost the same question.

One warning. The hypothetical version is a thinking tool, not a plan. Realistically, nobody gets a clean slate, the budget does not change, and you are stuck with three decisions somebody made before you arrived. What you do get is leverage: once you can describe the better version precisely, in one or two sentences, you can trade for a piece of it. You will not get two days of rehearsal. You might get four hours, and if those four hours are the right four hours, it is worth it. Every useful compromise in this industry started as somebody being able to say, clearly, what they would do if it were up to them.

choices: To argue that most production processes should be rebuilt from scratch.
To show why the hypothetical question gets honest answers, and what to do with them.
To explain how to negotiate a bigger budget with a client.

items.situation: Imagine you had a clean slate on a project you know well. Say what you would change first.
tips: If I had a clean slate, I would change the order of the week.
If + past, would + base verb. The past form here is not about the past.

items.situation: Now use the verb be, in the form the grammar prefers.
tips: If the budget were bigger, I would hire a second engineer.
Were with every subject: if I were, if she were, if the budget were.

items.situation: Give somebody advice using the classic phrase for it.
tips: If I were you, I would ask before Friday.
If I were you is the most common way a native speaker gives advice.

items.situation: Say what would probably happen, using a softer verb than would.
tips: If we rehearsed for two days, we might lose a day of editing.
Might for a possible result; would for a confident one.

items.situation: Say something honest about a decision, using the hypothetical.
tips: In hindsight, I would not have argued about it.
The hypothetical makes it safe to be honest. That is why the question works.

items.situation: Now name the realistic version: what you would actually trade for.
tips: Realistically I will not get two days, but four hours in the right place would be worth it.
Describe the better version precisely, then ask for the piece of it that is negotiable.

listenings.text: I ask everybody I work with the same question at the end of a project, and I have been doing it for about nine years. Not what went wrong, because that question makes people defend themselves and you learn nothing. The question is: if you did this again next month, with the same money, what would you do differently? And the difference in the answers is extraordinary. The first one puts people on trial. The second one makes them curious about their own work. Almost nobody says they would change the big thing. They say they would move one meeting. They say they would have brought the musical director into the room in week one instead of week three. And here is the part that surprised me for the first three years: if you collect twenty of those answers across twenty projects, you do not get twenty different problems. You get the same four, described by different people who all think they are the only one who noticed.

There is a trap in the hypothetical, and I fell into it for years, so let me name it. It is very satisfying to describe the perfect version of the job. If I had three more days. If the room were bigger. If somebody else had made that decision in two thousand nineteen. All of that is true, and none of it is useful on its own, because the room is the size it is and the decision was made. What changed things for me was one extra sentence, and I learned it from somebody who ran a studio for thirty years. She would listen to the whole beautiful description of the perfect version, and then she would say: fine, now what is the cheapest half of that? And there always is a cheapest half. If you want two extra days of rehearsal, you are not getting them. But the reason you want them is usually one specific thing, and that thing might cost four hours on a Tuesday. Describe the perfect version so that you can find the affordable piece of it. Do not describe it so that you can be right about what you were never going to get.

extra_audio.text: Pedro says that if he had a clean slate, he would not rebuild the whole system. He explains that he would change two decisions that were made in the first month. He says that if the budget were bigger, he would hire a second engineer for the live week. He adds that realistically nobody gets a clean slate, and that he is stuck with three constraints. He says that what he would trade for is four hours of rehearsal in the right place. Then he asks the other person what they would do differently.
